question: Is intermittent fasting better than calorie restriction for weight loss? Cite studies.
raw_answer:
Based on the provided sources, intermittent fasting is not shown to be better than calorie restriction for weight loss; instead, the studies indicate similar weight loss outcomes between the two approaches.

A randomized controlled trial found that time-restricted eating (a form of intermittent fasting) and calorie restriction produced similar weight loss over six months, with no significant difference in the amount of weight lost between the groups [3]. The study noted that while both methods led to comparable weight loss, the pathways to that outcome differed: calorie restriction led to increased self-control and reduced hunger, whereas time-restricted eating achieved similar results without requiring the same level of food-related discipline [3].

Another study involving night shift workers found no difference in weight loss after 18 months between those following modified intermittent fasting or daily calorie restriction, despite the fact that the intervention period lasted only 24 weeks and was followed by only limited support [4]. The authors concluded that both strategies were effective for long-term weight management, suggesting that the flexibility of the approach may be key to sustainability [4].

A separate 12-week study found that time-restricted eating led to modest weight loss (median 2.7%) even when calorie intake was kept consistent, with no significant difference compared to a 16-hour eating window [5]. This suggests that meal timing alone may contribute to weight loss, but not to a greater extent than calorie restriction when calorie intake is controlled.

Therefore, the evidence from these studies does not support that intermittent fasting is better than calorie restriction for weight loss; rather, they indicate comparable effectiveness [2][3][4][5].

passages.text: The goal of both strategies is to create a caloric deficit, meaning that your body uses more energy (calories) than it consumes, says Brynna Connor, MD, a board-certified family medicine physician in private practice in Austin, Texas, and healthcare ambassador at NorthWestPharmacy.com. To help clear up the debate between intermittent fasting versus calorie counting, we asked medical experts how these two methods compare and how to choose a suitable approach.

passages.heading: Intermittent Fasting vs. Calorie Counting: How They Work
passages.text: Both methods share the same goal of weight loss, but they go about it in different ways.

passages.heading: Effectiveness
passages.text: From a weight loss standpoint, intermittent fasting and calorie counting tend to produce similar results, Eid says. Some studies give intermittent fasting a slight edge, but the difference is usually modest and may have more to do with which plan people can follow consistently.

sources.title: A Simpler Alternative To Calorie Counting May Be Just As Effective

passages.heading: This Time-Based Eating Approach May Match Calorie Counting—Without The Mental Load
passages.text:
**Daily Harvest**/ Contributor

Weight loss strategies often get reduced to a simple equation of calories in versus calories out. But in real life, how we eat (the psychology behind food choices, hunger, and self-control) can matter just as much as the numbers on a plate.

A new randomized trial adds nuance to that picture, suggesting that intermittent fasting and traditional calorie restriction may lead to similar weight loss outcomes, but through distinctly different behavioral pathways that shape eating habits over time.

passages.heading: Same destination, very different journeys
passages.text:
Both groups lost similar amounts of weight by the end of the study. How they got there, though, was quite different.

The calorie-counting group became more disciplined around food over time. They reported greater control over their eating, lower hunger levels, and less overeating.

The fasting group reached the same weight-loss outcome with fewer of those psychological shifts. They did show some improvements in eating behavior, just not to the same degree as the calorie-counting group, and they got there without becoming more food-focused or restrictive.

They simply ate within a set time window. *A more prescriptive approach didn't lead to better results.*

passages.heading: The takeaway
passages.text:
A new study found that intermittent fasting with early time-restricted eating and daily calorie restriction produced similar weight loss over six months, but through very different experiences.

Calorie restriction made people more controlled and disciplined around food; fasting achieved the same results with fewer of those shifts, and without worsening mood, sleep, or quality of life over the long term.

If you've been assuming that more discipline equals better results, the more useful question may be which approach you can actually sustain.

sources.title: Weight loss maintenance one year after modified intermittent fasting in circadian-disrupted night shift workers: longer-term secondary outcomes from the SWIFt randomised clinical trial - Communications Medicine

passages.heading: Methods:
passages.text: We examined secondary 18-month outcomes of the SWIFt trial; a three-arm, parallel-group randomised controlled trial. Night-shift workers (*n* = 250) were randomised 1:1:1 to 24 weeks of moderate (20%) energy restriction; daily (continuous energy restriction; CER); or modified intermittent fasting on two days per week, undertaken on days off/day shifts (IF:2D) or during night shifts (IF:2N). The primary endpoint was reported previously. Outcomes of body weight, HOMA-IR and cardiometabolic risk factors were assessed 18 months after study enrolment, which was 12 months after completion of the supported intervention period. Analyses used the intention-to-treat principle. ANZCTR ACTRN-12619001035112 (19/07/2019).

passages.heading: Plain language summary
passages.text: People who work night shifts are at greater risk of overweight and obesity, yet little is known about which weight loss strategies are most effective over the long term. In the SWIFt trial, 250 shift workers were assigned to one of three dietary approaches for 24 weeks: daily calorie restriction, modified intermittent fasting on two days off or day shifts, or modified intermittent fasting on two night shifts. After completing the programme, participants received only limited support for a further 12 months. After 18 months, all groups had lost weight compared to when they enroled in the trial, with no difference seen between intermittent fasting or daily energy restriction. These findings suggest that lifestyle interventions that are flexible may help shift workers achieve sustainable long-term weight management.

sources.title: Study Finds Time-Restricted Eating Helped People Lose Weight Without Cutting Calories
sources.site_name: Study Finds Time-Restricted Eating Helped People Lose Weight Without Cutting Calories

passages.text:
**A shorter daily eating window was linked to improved eating habits, with no clear advantage in measured appetite hormones or inflammation markers.**

Time-restricted eating asks people to fit their meals into the same eight- to 10-hour window each day. Because people may also eat less on that schedule, researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine set out to test what happens when calorie intake stays consistent.

In their 12-week study, adults with obesity and either prediabetes or type 2 diabetes controlled through diet lost a modest amount of weight on a 10-hour eating schedule. Their median weight loss was 2.7%, nearly the same as the 2.5% among participants assigned a usual eating pattern spread over 16 hours. Both groups received meals with calorie amounts personalized to maintain their starting weights.

passages.heading: Separating meal timing from calorie cuts
passages.text:
Other studies of time-restricted eating have involved participants cutting calories, either intentionally or unintentionally, according to Duan. By keeping calorie intake consistent, her team could examine whether meal timing affected eating behavior, appetite hormones, or inflammation. The researchers wanted to understand whether benefits associated with time-based eating plans come from weight loss alone or also involve other biological mechanisms.

More than 100 million U.S. adults have obesity, and 115 million have prediabetes, in which blood sugar is elevated but remains below the diabetes range.

passages.heading: Separating meal timing from calorie cuts
passages.text:
These conditions increase the risk of complications such as high blood pressure, heart attack, and stroke, and the number of people affected is expected to grow. Intermittent fasting, which includes time-restricted eating, has broadly been linked to weight loss and may benefit people with either or both conditions. Its structured patterns of fasting and eating focus on when people eat rather than requiring calorie cuts or the avoidance of particular foods.

For the trial, researchers randomly assigned 19 adults to the 10-hour eating window and 20 to the 16-hour window. Participants were 18 to 69 years old, and the group was predominantly female (92%) and Black (92%).
